Very different long-term outcome.

This isn’t about skipping a mortgage payment.

It’s about understanding how timing works.

When you close on a home, interest starts building right away… even before your first scheduled payment.

Most people just follow the default payment date their lender gives them.

But depending on your closing date, adjusting that first payment to the start of the next month can sometimes reduce the amount of interest that builds up early on.

It’s a small detail, but small details can add up over time.

Every lender structures this a little differently, so it’s worth asking the question before you close.

Sometimes it’s not about doing anything complicated.

It’s just about knowing how the timing works.

Most people are trying to solve the wrong financial problem.

They think, “If I just made more money, everything would be easier.”

You simply don’t have enough coming in to comfortably cover your goals.

📉 2. Spending
Your lifestyle has quietly grown with your income, leaving little room to build wealth.

🏡 3. Debt Structure
Your mortgage, loans, or lines of credit may be costing you more than they need to or limiting your monthly cash flow.

🧾 4. Taxes
You’re paying more tax than necessary because no one is helping you plan ahead, not just file your return.

📈 5. Investments
You’ve done a great job saving, but your money isn’t working as efficiently as it could.

Here’s the interesting part…

Many people assume they have an income problem.

But I often meet families earning well into the six figures who actually have a debt structure, tax, or investment optimization problem. On the flip side, I’ve met people with more modest incomes who are quietly building wealth because they’ve optimized the pieces they can control.

The goal isn’t to optimize everything.

It’s to identify the one bottleneck that’s creating the biggest ripple effect.

That’s exactly where we come in.

Whether you’re buying your first home, renewing your mortgage, investing in real estate, our job is to help you identify the bottleneck that’s holding you back and build a plan around it.

caption:
The biggest mistake I see first-time buyers make isn’t waiting…

It’s comparing this month’s rent to this month’s mortgage payment.

That comparison misses almost everything that actually builds wealth.

When you own a home, several things can happen at the same time:

🏡 Part of every mortgage payment pays down your loan and builds equity.

📈 As your career progresses, your income often increases while your mortgage payment stays relatively stable (if you choose a fixed payment structure). Over time, that payment typically feels smaller relative to your income.

🏃‍➡️ Renting can create a treadmill effect. As your income grows, your rent often grows too. Many renters never feel like they’re getting ahead because a portion of every raise goes toward higher housing costs.

💰 If your home appreciates over the long term, that growth can add to your net worth while you’re simply living in it.

🇨🇦 And if it’s your principal residence, any qualifying capital gain when you sell is generally tax-free under current Canadian tax rules.

None of these benefits alone are guaranteed to make buying the right decision.

But together, over 10, 20 or 30 years, they can compound into a massive financial advantage.

That’s one reason why Statistics Canada found homeowners under 35 have a median net worth of roughly 10 times that of renters.

This doesn’t mean everyone should buy today.

It means you shouldn’t make one of the biggest financial decisions of your life based only on comparing this month’s payment.

The right question is:

What puts Future You in the strongest financial position?

A Mom messaged me recently in a bit of a panic because she received a letter saying her mortgage maturity date was coming up… and the bank wasn’t offering a renewal.

She asked me:

“Wait… can they actually do that?”

Short answer: yes.

Banks don’t have to renew a mortgage if something about the file has changed since you first qualified.

Things like:

• income changes
• higher debt levels
• missed payments
• property issues
• stricter lending rules
• internal risk policies

When she told me the story I joked:

“So they broke up with you.”

Not the best feeling.

But also not the end of the world.

Because one lender saying no doesn’t mean every lender will say no.

In situations like this there are often still options, like:

• refinancing with another lender
• extending amortization to improve cash flow
• changing mortgage structure
• working with lenders who specialize in renewal situations

The most important thing is time.

If you get a letter like this and still have 60 days before maturity, that’s usually enough time to explore solutions.

Where people get into trouble is waiting until the last minute.

caption:
Renovating your home? Read this before demo day.
Our full gut renovation starts next week.
Walls coming down. Floors ripped up. 4–6 months of chaos.
And then it hit us:
“We have home insurance… but do they even know what’s about to happen?”

Here’s something most homeowners don’t realize…
Major renovations change your insurance risk profile.
When a house is:
 • Under construction
 • Partially vacant
 • Missing walls, plumbing, or kitchens
 • Or not being lived in
…it is no longer insured the same way as a “normal” occupied home.
And if something happens during that time; fire, theft, water damage and your insurer wasn’t informed?
A claim can be denied.
Not because you did anything wrong…
but because the policy was never updated to match reality.

So here’s what we did (and what we recommend):
We called our insurance provider

Told them:
 – Renovations are starting
 – The home will be vacant during construction
 – It’s a full gut + rebuild

They updated the policy to a renovation / builder-risk endorsement

This usually:
 • Adds coverage for construction materials
 • Covers contractor liability
 • Protects you while the home is unlivable
 • And keeps your claims valid
It often costs a little more per month…
but it protects hundreds of thousands of dollars in risk.

We’re building a life, not just a house.
And part of that is protecting what we’re working so hard to create.
If you’re renovating, flipping, or converting a property right now, this is one of those quiet moves that saves you from loud problems later.

When we walk through an investment property, our mindset is totally different from when we’re house-hunting for ourselves.

We’re not chasing “dream home” energy, we’re looking for opportunity.

Here’s exactly what we look for 

1. Layout & Livability
Can we add a secondary suite or convert part of the home into a rental unit? A flexible floor plan often means more income potential.

We’re okay with updates that create equity, things like; new floors, kitchens, or paint. But if a property needs a new roof and foundation work, we make sure the numbers justify it.

3. Rental Demand
We check vacancy rates and comparable rents before we ever put in an offer. Cash flow isn’t about what we think it’ll rent for, it’s about what the market says.

We love seeing new cafes, schools, or transit projects nearby. These are signs that the area is on the rise, which usually means appreciation is coming next.

5. Exit Strategy
Before we buy, we’re already thinking about how we’ll eventually pull our money back out. Are we refinancing to reinvest, or holding long-term for steady cash flow?

Real estate investing isn’t about finding the perfect property.
It’s about finding the right opportunity and knowing how to make it work for your goals.

The Stock Market – Made Simple

Think of the stock market as a giant store where people buy and sell tiny pieces of companies.
Those pieces are called stocks.

When you buy a stock, you’re basically saying:

“I think this company’s gonna grow… and I want a cut when it does.”

It’s like your friend starts a business, you give her $100, and now you own 1% of her profits. That’s what buying a stock is, except instead of your friend, it’s Apple, Nike, or Lululemon.

How the price changes
• The more people want a stock, the more valuable it becomes.
• Think Stanley Cups: they went viral, sold for $80 on Amazon… then hype faded, and now they’re $30–$40 at Walmart.

How you make money (2 ways):
1. Buy low, sell high: Purchase when it’s cheaper, sell later when others will pay more.
2. Dividends: Some companies literally pay you just for owning their stock. This is their way of sharing profits and rewarding loyal shareholders.

Example:
• Pepsi or Rogers = stable profits → pay dividends.
• Skims = growing fast → reinvests profits into expansion → no dividends (yet).

It’s not gambling, it’s ownership.
You’re either getting a share of the profits today, or betting on bigger profits tomorrow.

Have you ever noticed that no matter how much more money you start making… it still feels like you’re living paycheck to paycheck?

Guilty! 🙋🏽‍♂️

Basically, when my income goes up, my spending goes up too. It happens to us all, bigger homes, nicer cars, more vacations. And before I knew it, my savings don’t actually grow.

And it’s not just lifestyle creep. To make it worse, I don’t even have a financial plan. Instead I was hoping my money will ‘work itself out,’ but without clear goals, it usually doesn’t.

Then there’s the keeping up with the Joneses effect, buying things to match the lifestyle of friends or coworkers. New cars, designer bags, the whole image game.

Add in poor financial habits like: impulse spending, avoiding bank statements, or fearing the idea of investing and suddenly, even with a higher salary, you’re stuck in the same cycle of stress and debt.

So how did I break from it?

First, I set a plan. Set financial goals that give my money a purpose.

 Second, had to slow my spending rate. The growth could not keep up with my earnings. If I you get a raise, I would commit a big chunk of it straight to savings or investments.

 Third, automate it, so the money is moved before I can touch it.

 And lastly, redefine what a reward looks like. Instead of chasing the quick high of a purchase, focus on the long-term freedom of building wealth.

Because at the end of the day, it’s not how much you make. It’s how much you keep and what you do with it…that creates real financial freedom

caption:
Ever wonder why even people making good money still feel like they’re never getting ahead?

A lot of it comes down to habits. Not the big mistakes those little damn sneaky ones that drain your future freedom.

Here are 5 common money habits that keep people trapped, and how to flip them so you can build real momentum:

Habits That Keep You Stuck

Ignoring your real spending
You know what I mean… you glance at your bank account, see the balance, and hope the rest takes care of itself. Nope. Without tracking what you actually spend, your money slips through the cracks.

Paying only minimums on debt
Minimum payments are illusions of progress. Debt repayment that drags on quietly costs you thousands in interest. That’s money you could use for your future.

Skipping savings in “good times”
When you earn more, most people treat it like a raise, not an opportunity. The richer your income grows, the bigger your lifestyle jumps. Save first. Spend second.

Chasing convenience, not value
Same-day delivery. Subscription after subscription. Impulse purchases. Luxury upgrades. They all add up, but rarely add joy or freedom.

Waiting for the “perfect moment”
“Wait till payday.” 
“Wait till I have an emergency fund.” 
“Wait till rates drop.” 
Life rarely lines up perfectly. 
Momentum beats perfection.

How To Flip The Script

Start by tracking every dollar for 1 month. Spare your “embarrassing” expenses, they’ll show you where leaks are.

Prioritize debts that drain you most (high interest, short payoff) and throw extra at them when possible.

Automate your savings, even $50 a week counts.

Trim or pause subscriptions. 
Question recurring purchases.

Set a target “starter move,” one real estate opportunity, one investment, or simply locking a better rate. Do that before waiting for everything to be ideal.

Progress doesn’t require perfect finances, it requires consistent effort in the right direction. If you stop doing what’s easy and start doing what moves you forward, freedom finds you.

caption:
Let’s talk about why going 50/50 on everything in a relationship might not be the fairest way to split expenses.

When Caro and I first moved in together, splitting everything down the middle made sense. We were both working, both contributing. It felt fair.

But things changed.

She started making more money than me, and suddenly my half of the bills left me with nothing. 
No room to save, no extra for leisure, and definitely not enough for things like date nights or surprises — which I wanted to do.

So I brought up the idea of equity over equality.

Instead of splitting 50/50, we calculate our total household expenses and each contribute a percentage based on our income. That way, it still feels equal — but it’s also sustainable and fair.

Here’s a mock example:
🎯 Equity Split Example

👫 Household Income: $100,000
💰 Partner A: $65,000
💰 Partner B: $35,000
🏡 Total Household Expenses: $30,000/year (or $2,500/month)

⸻

📊 Step 1: Calculate Income Percentages
	•	Partner A (65k):
$65,000 ÷ $100,000 = 65% of the income
	•	Partner B (35k):
$35,000 ÷ $100,000 = 35% of the income

⸻

💸 Step 2: Apply Percentages to Expenses
	•	Partner A Pays:
65% of $30,000 = $19,500/year
→ $1,625/month
	•	Partner B Pays:
35% of $30,000 = $10,500/year
→ $875/month

With this model we both felt more comfortable and it felt more fair. It encouraged us to earn more than the other, like a competition of sorts. 

Ever had this convo with your partner? ❤️

💫Everyone talks about biweekly mortgage payments like it’s the holy grail for saving interest.

✅ Yes — switching from monthly to biweekly can save you tens of thousands and shave years off your mortgage.

BUT… here’s what most people don’t know 👇

When you increase your regular mortgage payments — even with good intentions — you’re also increasing your officially registered obligation with your lender.

⚠️ This means you may reduce your ability to qualify for future investment properties, second homes, or even refinances…

In other words: that extra payment might save you a little now, but cost you opportunities later.

💡 A Smarter Move?

Make lump sum payments on your own terms (if your lender allows it). This…

• Keeps your official payment lower
• Gives you flexibility in case of emergencies
• Protects your borrowing capacity for future deals

💡 Why lump sum payments (vs increasing regular payments) can be the smarter move for real estate investors:
	1.	Borrowing Power Preservation 🧠
When you increase your regular payment, that higher monthly obligation becomes officially recorded on your credit profile. Lenders use your monthly debt obligations to calculate how much more you can borrow.
→ Higher monthly payment = Lower room to borrow more.
	2.	Emergency Flexibility 🛑
Life happens. If you lock into higher regular payments, you’re committed—even during months when cash might be tight.
→ Lump sum = optional. You pay more when you can, not because you have to.
	3.	Strategic Wealth Building 📈
Investors play the long game. Preserving liquidity and borrowing capacity means you can jump on the next deal when it comes.
→ Lump sums let you pay down debt AND stay nimble.
	4.	Avoid Requalifying Headaches 🧾
If you change your payment structure officially and later want to reverse it, you often have to requalify with the lender, which may not always be easy.
→ Lump sums keep things simple.

caption:
“Why did my property taxes jump AFTER I bought my home? 😫🏡”

You budgeted for your mortgage. You even accounted for taxes.
So why are your monthly costs suddenly higher than expected?

Here’s what most homeowners aren’t told:

When you buy a home, your mortgage lender estimates your property taxes based on the previous owner’s bill — not what you’ll actually owe long-term.

But once the home sells (and especially if you renovate), your property is likely reassessed — meaning the tax man updates the value… and your bill.

➡️ Higher assessed value = higher taxes
➡️ If you pay taxes through your lender, you may fall into a shortfall
➡️ That means your monthly payments increase to cover the new taxes + the shortfall

It’s not a penalty — it’s just how the system works.
But if you don’t see it coming, it can feel like a punch to your budget.

Pro tip: Build in a buffer during your first year of homeownership to prepare for this jump.

caption:
🚨 So you’re ready to invest in real estate?
STOP.

Before you do anything else, you need to understand the one metric that determines how far you can scale your portfolio:

👉 LVR – Loan to Value Ratio

Here’s why it matters:

🔍 What is LVR?

It’s the ratio of your loan amount to the value of the property.

✅ If you put 20% down and the bank lends you 80%, your LVR is 80%.
That’s the sweet spot — most lenders won’t go higher.

But what happens when the value of your property goes UP?
Your LVR goes DOWN.
That’s a good thing — because it unlocks equity you can use to buy the next property.

🏡 Let’s say you buy at $500K with a $400K loan (LVR = 80%)
Over time, or through renovations, the value rises to $650K.
Your loan is still $400K…
Now your LVR is 61%.

That 19% difference?
That’s leverageable equity.
Which means you can refinance and pull out cash to buy another property — without saving a new down payment.

🔥 This is how smart investors scale fast
They understand how to:
✅ Keep LVR under 80%
✅ Force appreciation
✅ Leverage equity strategically
✅ Avoid over-leveraging and keep the banks happy

💰 You don’t need a massive salary or giant savings.
You just need to understand how to use LVR to your advantage.

Here’s exactly how to build your emergency fund quickly and smartly:

SPENDING 🛑  1️⃣ Cut discretionary expenses or Boost Income  Audit your subscriptions, takeout, shopping, and entertainment. Slash ruthlessly. Redirect every saved dollar into your emergency fund. (Tip: Download and audit your last months banking/credit reports to instantly spot what to keep vs. cut.) Small side hustles, overtime, selling services, or even a weekend gig—channel all extra cash straight into your fund. If you find a way to make more, you don’t need to cut.
2️⃣ Delay big purchases.  New car? Major reno? Fancy tech? Hit pause. Big expenses come with hidden “phantom costs” you don’t see upfront. Play defense right now on the big purchases that don’t make you money.
3️⃣ Stretch your regular spending.  Push out personal care like haircuts, spa visits, even clothing buys. Stretch those cycles longer — small tweaks = big savings over a year. Especially if you have a large family with kids. Can you delay or cut their hair at home (like my mom used to). Buy second hand clothes - this is something we do all year round. 

INVESTMENTS 💰  4️⃣ Prioritize saving over low-interest debt payments.  If you’re overpaying your 3% mortgage, stop. It’s smarter to stack cash now than rush to be “debt-free.” Your emergency fund is your top priority.
5️⃣ Temporarily scale back retirement contributions.  If you’re in a riskier position (single income, kids, etc.), consider reducing RRSP/401 contributions — just enough to still get the company match if you have one. A few months won’t wreck your future, but a lack of savings could wreck your present.
6️⃣ Create and Separate the Account. Keep your emergency fund in a separate, easy-to-access (but not too easy) high-yield savings account.

Out of sight = out of mind = faster growth.

Peace of mind is priceless — and the faster you build it, the faster you can focus on growing wealth instead of putting out fires. 

Final Thought:  You can’t predict the next emergency.  But you can prepare for it.
Every dollar you save today is one less thing to panic about tomorrow.
Start today — your future self will be grateful. 🙏

Person B – The Investor Mindset

🔄 Repeat this process, and they build multiple appreciating, cash-flowing properties that pay for their lifestyle.

The Bottom Line
💡 Person A has a beautiful home but remains financially stuck.  💰 Person B builds wealth, financial freedom, and early retirement.

❌ Uncertain Appreciation – If your market isn’t growing, your home value might stagnate or even decline. Inflation can outpace appreciation.
❌ Illiquidity – Need cash? Selling a home takes time, and you might be forced to accept a lower price in a downturn.
❌ Opportunity Cost – Your equity is locked up. Instead of sitting in your home, it could be earning higher returns elsewhere.
❌ Emotional vs. Financial Decisions – People buy homes for lifestyle, stability, and comfort—not for maximizing returns.
❌ Equity Growth Requires Selling – The only way to tap into your home’s value is to sell or refinance, meaning your wealth isn’t easily accessible.

Want to build REAL wealth? 💸 Buy investment properties that cash flow, appreciate, and put money in your pocket every month.

Your primary home is where you live—not where you get rich. 📈

No Holding Back—How to Start Investing in Real Estate (Step by Step) 🚀

If you’re serious about investing, here’s the roadmap:
🔹 Step 1: Evaluate Your Resources & Goals
* What do you want? Cash flow, appreciation, or quick refinancing?
* How much time, capital, and borrowing power do you have?
* Define your end goal before making your first move.

🔹 Step 2: Pick ONE Investing Strategy & Stick to It
* Don’t jump between strategies—master one.
* Want passive investing? Avoid active strategies like short-term rentals.
* Each strategy has tricks, formulas, and hacks—focus on learning them to scale faster.

🔹 Step 3: Choose the Right City
* Pick a city that fits your strategy.
* Look for hospitals, universities, and major employers—these markets stay strong.
* Choose a location where you can pivot if needed.

🔹 Step 4: Connect with an Investor-Friendly Realtor
* Find an agent who invests themselves—they’ll know the game.
* Build a team that understands investment real estate.

🔹 Step 5: Find a Cash-Flowing Property
* If you want to scale, aim for rents at least 2X your mortgage payment.
* Strong cash flow = financial cushion + more borrowing power for future deals.

caption:
🚀 5 Critical Steps to Take After Selling Your Home

Congrats on closing your home sale! But before you kick back, here’s what you need to prioritize to protect your profits and plan your next move 👇

1️⃣ Lock in Your Finances
✅ Settle outstanding costs – Ensure closing fees, commissions, and any remaining mortgage balances are paid.
✅ Secure your proceeds – Put funds to a high-interest savings account or investment vehicle while planning your next steps.
✅ Understand tax implications –  principal residence is tax-exempt from capital gains. If reporting gains, explore tax-saving strategies.

2️⃣ Notify and Update All Relevant Parties
📬 Change your address – Update it with banks, government agencies, subscriptions, and service providers.
🔌 Transfer or cancel utilities & services – Ensure hydro, gas, internet, and other services are updated or stopped.
🏠 Adjust insurance coverage – cancel, transfer, or adjust your home insurance policy.

3️⃣ Plan Your Next Move
🏡 Secure your next living arrangement- make sure you have a plan in place.
📦 Plan your move – Book movers, a truck and get help early to avoid last-minute stress.
🚀 Transition strategically – reinvesting in real estate? Start scouting 

4️⃣ Safeguard Important Documents
📑 Keep records of your sale agreement, closing documents, and tax receipts.
💰 Maintain records of renovations & upgrades – This helps with tax deductions or boosting resale value 

5️⃣ Put Your Profits to Work
💡 Reinvest in real estate – Expand your rental portfolio, or look into passive income properties.
📈 Diversify your investments – Consider stocks, bonds, or alternative ways to grow your wealth.
🎯 Align with your long-term goals – Whether it’s retirement, travel, business, or financial independence, your next steps should support your bigger vision.

🏡The Best Location to Invest In🤯

A great location can make or break your real estate investment. 

Here’s how to find one that sets you up for success:

✅ The Starbucks Strategy – Starbucks spends millions researching where to open new locations. If they’re moving in, chances are the area is growing and thriving—follow their lead.
✅ Neighborhood Safety – Check AreaVibes.com for crime rates, amenities, and livability scores. A neighborhood with a score of 70+ is typically a safe bet.
✅ Strong School Districts – Properties in top-rated school zones tend to hold value better and attract families & high-quality tenants who stay longer.
✅ Google Maps Hack – Do a virtual drive-by using Google Street View to explore the area before making a trip. Look for well-maintained properties, businesses, and infrastructure.
✅ Population & Employment Growth – Target areas with 40,000+ people and strong job markets. Proximity to major employers, hospitals, and universities makes rentals more in demand.

💡 A great location makes everything easier—higher demand, better tenants, and long-term appreciation. 

Do your research and invest where the fundamentals are strong!

caption:
🚨Myth: You Can Retire Quick Off Real Estate 🚨

💭 Many people think real estate is an overnight ticket to wealth—buy a few properties, sit back, and retire early. But here’s the truth…

🏡 Reality: Real Estate is a Get-Rich-For-Sure Plan, NOT a Get-Rich-Quick Scheme.
✅ It Takes Work: Finding the right deals, securing financing, and managing properties requires effort. Success doesn’t happen by accident.
✅ It Requires Skills: You need to analyze deals, negotiate, manage tenants, and leverage financing. The more skills you develop, the faster you grow.
✅ Time is Your Friend: Wealth in real estate is built through cash flow, mortgage paydown, appreciation, and tax advantages. These things compound over time, not overnight.
✅ Market Cycles Matter: Prices don’t always go up instantly. The real winners play the long game and buy assets that will grow in value over decades.

💡 The Path to True Financial Freedom:
* Work Hard: Treat real estate like a business, not a hobby.
* Accelerate Growth: Reinvest your profits into more assets.
* Leverage Smartly: Use other people’s money (OPM) to scale faster.
* Replace Your Income: Build enough passive cash flow to cover your lifestyle.

📢 Retire WITH Real Estate, Not FROM It.
 Real estate isn’t an escape from work—it’s a vehicle to control your time, wealth, and freedom.
